set.st: A Menomonie paper of December 1880 described the remains of an old French stockade on a rise overlooking Rice Lake and its outlet, at a spot the Indians called Pocagama, said to have been the post of a fur trader named August Borot, killed there by the Sioux about a century before. Barron County settlers had dug into the earth in several places nearby for the murdered Frenchman's buried cash; a neighbour, James Bracklin, dug up only a sharpened stake. The 1881 county history tells of the elder Cadot's post and grave near Rice Lake, which is the same tradition under another name. A visitor who walked the ground on 7 October 1880 wrote to the Wisconsin State Journal that the work lay about a mile southeast of Rice Lake village in section 27 of T35N R11W: a ditched enclosure about 50 feet square with turrets at the corners, hearth stones, charcoal and bones inside. Pin is the section, not the stockade.
set.pl: Sec 27 T35N R11W, a mile southeast of Rice Lake village, overlooking the lake and its outlet; the earthwork itself is not yet fixed inside the section
pinev: Section 27 T35N R11W from an 1880 eyewitness letter (Wisconsin State Journal, 16 Nov 1880); pin at the section centroid (BLM WI460350N0110W0SN27, 45.4799-45.4952, -91.7253 to -91.7042), r900. Formerly at the Red Cedar outlet.
